Patient-reported symptoms:

  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Sixty-three-year-old Margit had been a sculptor for nearly four decades, her hands as familiar with clay and stone as with her own skin. She had always worked alone in her studio, a converted garage behind the house she shared with her husband, Thomas. That solitude, once a sanctuary, had become a cage. The assault happened two years ago, late on a November evening, when a man she had known casually from the local arts council followed her home from an opening. He had offered to help carry equipment. She had trusted him. Inside the studio, he had locked the door and raped her while she begged him to stop. He had not said much, but he had whispered something about how she had “wanted it,” how she had “led him on.” Those words had lodged themselves inside her like splinters. She had not screamed. She had frozen. And that frozen compliance, that silence, had become the thing she could not forgive herself for.

In the months that followed, Margit’s world contracted. She stopped answering the phone when the arts council called. She deleted emails from colleagues. She told Thomas she was just tired, that her back hurt from the heavy lifting. But what she could not tell him—what she could barely admit to herself—was that she now felt safest only within the four walls of her bedroom, with the door locked and the blinds drawn. The studio, once her lifeblood, became a place of dread. Just walking past the garage door made her stomach drop. She had come to believe that she had done something fundamentally wrong that night, that her own body had betrayed her by not fighting, and that the man had seen something in her—some weakness, some invitation—that she herself could not see. She was certain that if she had been a stronger person, a better person, she would have screamed, would have clawed, would have stopped him. Instead, she had acted in a way that went against everything she believed about herself. She felt violated not only by him, but by her own response.

The people who should have protected her had not. She had reported the assault to the police, and the detective had asked her, twice, what she had been wearing. He had said, gently, that the case would be difficult to prove. No charges were filed. The institutional failure had hollowed out her trust in the world. She no longer believed that justice existed, or that anyone would believe her if she told the truth. This had drained the meaning from her work. She had once believed that sculpture was a way of making permanent what was beautiful and true. Now, nothing felt meaningful anymore. She had not touched clay in eighteen months. Her hands ached with the absence of it, but she could not bring herself to enter the studio. She had told Thomas she was struggling with “creative block,” but the block was not creative—it was terror.

Her avoidance had consequences that crept into every corner of her life. She had stopped attending openings, stopped seeing friends, stopped going to the grocery store after dark. When a siren wailed past the house, she would freeze mid-sentence, her heart hammering, her mind instantly back in the studio, hearing the lock click. She had become vigilant to unexpected movement. If Thomas walked into the kitchen too quickly, she would flinch, her hands flying up, and then she would feel ashamed of her own startle reflex. She had begun to feel a pervasive sense of shame and guilt that colored everything. She would catch herself thinking, *I am dirty now. I am ruined.* And the worst part was that she could not stop the thoughts from circling: *Nothing matters anymore. Why does any of this matter?*

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment that broke through her numbness. Last week, a young woman at the post office was talking loudly on her phone about a sexual assault case in the news. Margit had to leave the line, trembling, and had sat in her car for twenty minutes before she could drive home. That night, she told Thomas, for the first time, that she was not okay. She said she needed to talk to someone. She is sitting in my office now, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, her eyes fixed on the floor. She is afraid that talking about it will make it real again, that she will fall apart and never come back. But she is also afraid of staying like this—afraid of a life that has no studio, no clay, no meaning. She wants to know if it is possible to feel safe in more than one room again. She wants to know if she can ever forgive herself for freezing.
